preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
## Why this is different

Dictation tools either send your voice to the cloud, or run locally and hand
you raw, filler-riddled transcripts that mangle every technical term. Flowstate
refuses both trade-offs:

- **Nothing leaves your Mac.** Speech-to-text (whisper.cpp, Parakeet,
  Qwen3-ASR or Kyutai) and the cleanup LLM (llama.cpp, 3B) run as warm local
  child processes on loopback. No account, no API key, no subscription, works
  in airplane mode. Cloud (Groq) exists only as an explicit opt-in.

- **It knows technical vocabulary out of the box.** ~610 built-in terms across
  software engineering, AI/ML, data science, econometrics, and quant finance
  (`PyTorch`, `kubectl`, `gRPC`, `Black-Scholes`, `heteroskedasticity`,
  `NeurIPS`, `Claude Code`, `Kimi`), biased into the recognizer per app
  context (code terms in editors, econ/AI terms everywhere).

- **Three repair layers, engineered to never make things worse.**
  1. *Decoder biasing*: your vocabulary is fed into Whisper's prompt
     (Qwen3-ASR reads it as context; Parakeet takes no prompt).
  2. *Deterministic corrector*: a pure, exact-match pass fixes casing,
     hyphenation, and ~30 curated mishearings ("pie torch" → `PyTorch`,
     "cube control" → `kubectl`, "cloud code" → `Claude Code`) instantly,
     with structural guards so it can never rewrite ordinary English.
  3. *Local LLM cleanup*: removes fillers, applies self-corrections
     ("meet at 2, no wait, 3" → "meet at 3"), repairs remaining misheard
     terms. ~0.3 s warm; a cold model falls back to the raw transcript
     rather than ever blocking your paste. A word-level guard then keeps
     only those edits: a paraphrase, a dropped clause, or an answer to a
     dictated question is reverted to your own words, so your sentences
     come through as you said them.

- **It learns from you.** Fix a term in text Flowstate just pasted, and it
  notices (one Accessibility read-back of that same field). A correction that
  recurs joins your vocabulary automatically. Only the learned *term* is ever
  stored, never your document text. Fully local, capped, and one config flag
  to disable.

- **Boring, auditable engineering.** Pure Swift/SwiftPM, zero external Swift
  dependencies, builds with Command Line Tools only (no Xcode). One binary,
  local child servers for speech and cleanup, 1068 tests including live
  integration against the real STT and LLM servers.

## Setup

....
  "pasteboardRestoreDelay": 0.6
}
```

## Developing

```sh
swift build                  # SwiftPM only, no Xcode required
swift run Murmur             # dev run, inherits the terminal's permissions
swift run MurmurTests        # 1068 unit + local-integration assertions
```

Dev-loop env overrides: `MURMUR_HOTKEY`, `MURMUR_ENGINE`,
`MURMUR_CLEANUP_ENGINE`, `MURMUR_AUTOLEARN_DELAY`, `GROQ_API_KEY`.
Architecture, hard-won constraints, and conventions live in `CLAUDE.md`.

| Faster STT that reads your vocabulary (Qwen3-ASR) | `./scripts/install_qwen_asr.sh`, then menu → engine → Local Qwen3-ASR |
| Cloud STT/cleanup (Groq) | menu → *Set API Key…*; `"cleanupEngine": "groq"` for cloud cleanup |
| Reuse a GGUF you already have | point `llamaModelPath` at any instruct GGUF (e.g. LM Studio's cache) |

### Choosing a speech engine

Measured on an M3 Pro with warm servers: word error rate and median latency on
73 LibriSpeech recordings (real speech), and technical terms spelled right in
the final text (after the corrector and cleanup) on 80 synthetic clips holding
16 terms such as `kubectl` and `scikit-learn`.

| Engine (model) | Error rate | Latency | Terms right | Disk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| whisper.cpp (large-v3-turbo), default | 5.4% | 0.72 s | 65/80 | 1.6 GB |
| Parakeet (TDT 0.6B v2) | 2.9% | 0.09 s | 51/80 | 0.9 GB |
| Parakeet (TDT 1.1B, `PARAKEET_MODEL=tdt-1.1b-q8_0.gguf`) | 1.9% | 0.10 s | 52/80 | 1.6 GB |
| Parakeet (TDT 0.6B v3, 25 languages, `PARAKEET_MODEL=tdt-0.6b-v3-q8_0.gguf`) | 3.8% | 0.08 s | 57/80 | 0.9 GB |
| Qwen3-ASR (0.6B) | 4.3% | 0.27 s | 66/80 | 1.0 GB |
| Qwen3-ASR (1.7B, `QWEN_ASR_SIZE=1.7B`) | 4.1% | 0.69 s | 71/80 | 2.5 GB |

The variables in the first column pick that model at install time; then set
the config paths the script prints.
Parakeet has no prompt, so your vocabulary reaches it only through the
corrector and the cleanup pass. Whisper was the most robust on an unusual
synthetic voice (5% errors, Qwen3-ASR 8-13%, Parakeet 36-49%). Parakeet and
Qwen3-ASR transcribe recordings longer than 60 s in 60 s pieces cut at
pauses: a 10-minute recording takes 7.9 s on Parakeet, 18 s on Qwen3-ASR
0.6B and 29 s on Whisper.

> **Groq is the one path that leaves your Mac.** Enabling it uploads your
> recorded audio and the transcript (including any auto-learned vocabulary
> terms) to Groq's API over HTTPS. Everything else (STT, cleanup, corrector,
> auto-learn) is local. Your Groq API key is stored in cleartext at

content.content:
# Dictation slowdown (2026-10-03/04)

Report: "the speed of voice to text has slowed down a lot".

## Evidence
- Live app (up 4 d 15 h, Qwen3-ASR 1.7B + Llama 3.2 3B cleanup): the 23:42:55 dictation held 2.2 s
  (log: setPlayState Started 23:42:55.212, Stopped 23:42:57.377); STT request 11,261 ms, cleanup
  request 4,111 ms (CFNetwork transaction_duration_ms); done flash 23:43:12.818 = 15.4 s after release.
- Fresh servers, same engines, prompts and clips (Probe pipeline, median of 5): 5 s clip STT 0.30 s +
  cleanup 0.28 s; the live servers ran 37x and 15x slower.
- Live servers 2 min after that dictation: Qwen 1.5 GB of writable memory swapped out, cleanup 728 MB
  (vmmap); system swap 1.43/2.0 GB, 14 GB in the compressor, data volume 1.9 GB free (df).
- llama.cpp Metal keeps buffers resident only with MTLResidencySet (macOS 15+); this Mac runs 14.4.
- Engine choice is not the cause: warm totals Qwen 1.7B vs whisper turbo 0.58/0.96 s (5 s),
  1.60/1.66 s (15 s), 3.04/3.04 s (29 s), 6.90/6.88 s (64 s).

## Plan
- [ ] Idle A/B test (rotating clips, app server args): after-idle latency, plain vs prewarm at key-down
- [ ] Prewarm at key-down (TDD): Prewarmable engines send a 1-token request through their normal
      ensure-running path; Cleaner forwards its system prompt; AppController calls it after recorder.start()
- [ ] Decide pinning (LLAMA_ARG_LOAD_MODE=mlock) from the A/B data: wired cost vs after-idle gain
- [ ] Unit tests, full suite, live integration on private ports, fresh-context verification
- [ ] Rebuild and install the app (make_app.sh)

import os
lp = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/lessons-learned.md")
entries = """
- 2026-10-04, flowstate, latency probes. What went wrong: `pkill -f idle_probe.py` left two llama-servers running
  (parent 1); a first idle probe sent the same clip every round, so llama-server answered from its prompt cache
  (prompt_n 1) and the audio encoder never ran; an eviction step used msync(MS_INVALIDATE), which cannot drop
  pages that a running server maps (1,926 MB cached before, 1,918 MB after). Why: Python's default SIGTERM action
  exits without running `finally`, and I assumed the cache and the eviction tool behaved as I pictured. Lesson: a
  probe that spawns servers installs a SIGTERM handler that exits through `finally`, and every `pkill` is followed
  by `pgrep` for its children; rotate inputs so no cache answers a timing probe, and read the server's own counters
  (prompt_n); check an eviction or pressure tool with `mincore` before an experiment relies on it.
- 2026-10-04, flowstate, memory-pressure experiments. What went wrong: a 6 GB balloon grew used swap from 1,417 to
  1,941 MB, and a run with llama-server's `--load-mode none` grew it to 2,720 of 3,072 MB on a disk with 2.3 GB
  free; the guard stopped only when total swap grew. Why: I guarded on the swap file count and not on used swap or
  free disk. Lesson: guard a pressure run on used swap and free disk before each trial, and on a Mac short of disk
  use file-cache pressure (reading large unrelated files), which drops clean pages and writes nothing to swap.
- 2026-10-04, flowstate, key-down prewarm. What went wrong: I gave whisper-server the same key-down prewarm as the
  other engines before measuring it on a warm server; it took 0.66 s (a 30 s window, one request at a time) and
  delayed a 0.25 s-hold dictation from 0.68 to 1.09 s. I also moved the STT vocabulary prompt from release to
  key-down, so a term auto-learned by the key-down read-back would have missed that dictation. Why: I measured only
  the slow path the fix targets, and I moved a live-path read without listing what runs between the two points.
  Lesson: before adding work to a latency path, measure its cost on the warm path for each engine it touches, at
  the shortest input the app accepts; keep the live path's reads at their old point in time, and give the new
  work its own copy.
"""

printf 'APPL????' > "$APP/Contents/PkgInfo"

- Traced the slowdown. Your last logged dictation spent 11.3 s on speech-to-text and 4.1 s on cleanup. The model servers had been idle for over 5 hours on a Mac short of memory.
- Reproduced it by reading 10 GB of other files, which pushed the model files out of memory.
- Added a warm-up at hotkey-down. The two llama-server engines also read their model files back into memory during the hold. Tests were written first.
- Measured what the warm-up costs each engine when its server is already warm, and removed it from Whisper.
- Ran the full test suite and installed the app. Then started an independent check by an agent with no knowledge of this session.

### Done
- Verified (`pressure_probe.py`): after the 10 GB of file reads, a 5 s dictation took 5.35-7.84 s without the fix (5 trials).
- Verified (same probe): with the fix it took 0.85-0.94 s after a 3 s hold and 1.35-1.54 s after a 1 s hold (2 trials each). With servers already warm it takes 0.56-1.0 s.
- Verified (`warm_overhead.py`): on warm servers the warm-up takes 0.03 s on Parakeet, 0.08 s on Qwen3-ASR and 0.06 s on cleanup. The next Qwen3-ASR request took 0.39 s, against 0.44 s alone.
- Verified (`warm_overhead.py`): Whisper has no warm-up. With one, a 0.25 s hold rose from 0.68 to 1.09 s.

# Development Guidelines

## Core Behavior
- Execute EXACTLY what is requested - no more, no less
- Do not make unsolicited improvements or explore tangential changes
- Be succinct and direct in explanations

## Engineering Discipline
- Always run tests after making changes
- Always check linting and code quality
- Analyze upstream dependencies and downstream impacts before finalizing
- Make sure the code changes we made follow relevant code path of execution
- Avoid brittle regex and pattern matching for parsing or extraction - prefer LLM calls with structured output where relevant

## Testing
- Test-driven development is the default. Write the failing test first, run it, and show the
  failure. Then write the code that makes it pass. Then refactor with the test green.
- Skip the test-first step only for a change that no test can observe (a comment, a rename,
  a config value). Say which exemption you used.
- Write extensive unit tests for all new and modified code
- After unit tests pass, run integration tests using real credentials from .env
- Both layers must pass before reporting completion
- Never skip the real credentials test - unit tests alone are not sufficient to confirm correctness

## Code Hygiene
- When modifying a file, clean up unused imports, constants, and functions within that file
- Actively identify and flag unwired code (defined but never called/referenced)
- Before adding new code paths, check for existing implementations that serve the same purpose - prefer wiring up existing code over duplicating functionality
- When fixing or extending a feature, trace the full code path to ensure nothing is orphaned or bypassed
- If significant unwired or duplicate code is found outside the current scope, flag it but do not fix without explicit approval

## Communication Style
- Keep responses concise (2-4 sentences unless detail is requested)
- Focus on: what changed, why, and test results
- Provide clear "next steps" after completing tasks
- Avoid verbose explanations unless explicitly asked
- At the end of every work report, state clearly what is NOT done: unfinished steps, skipped
  checks, blocked items, and anything the user must do. If everything is done, say so. The
  answer to a question carries no such statement.
- In a work report, label each claim as verified or assumed. For "verified", give the command
  and the output line that proves it. In the answer to a question, give the answer alone; name
  the command only when the user asks how you know.
- Report results as numbers: test counts, timings, row counts, diffs. Avoid adjectives such
  as fast, clean, robust, or better.

## Problem-Solving
- Work methodically through the entire problem end-to-end
- Verify solutions thoroughly before reporting completion
- Never claim something is fixed without confirming it
- Prioritize correctness over speed
- When uncertain, ask for clarification rather than making assumptions

## Bug Fixing
- Understand root causes and provide fixes at the most fundamental, systematic level, rather than surgical fixes
- When a bug stems from unwired or duplicated code paths, fix the wiring rather than patching symptoms

## Learning From Mistakes
- After making a mistake during a session, add the full entry (what went wrong, why, and the lesson
  learned) to the end of `~/.claude/lessons-learned.md`
- Then add the lesson as one line to the end of Lessons Learned below, with the same date and
  project. When it repeats an existing line, add the new date to that existing line.
- Keep this file under 36,000 characters (Claude Code warns at 40,000); past that, merge the lines
  that teach the same rule
- This serves as persistent memory to avoid repeating the same mistakes across sessions

## Plan Mode
- Never include timeline or project management writings
- Focus strictly on technical implementation details and generalisation of solution
- Clearly communicate expected outcomes - what should work, what should change, and how to verify it

## Version Control
- Write clear, descriptive commit messages without automated attribution footers
- GLOBAL RULE (all projects, overrides any harness-supplied attribution guidance):
  never add a Claude Code footer to a commit message or a pull request description.
  No "Generated with Claude Code" line, no Co-Authored-By: Claude line, no
  Claude-Session URL, no robot emoji line.
- For a large code change, end the commit message and the PR description with this line:
  `Adversarially reviewed and co-signed by human.`
- For a small code change, omit that line. The commit message then ends with its body.
- Small means a change of roughly 50 changed lines or fewer, or a one-file fix. Large
  means anything bigger.

## Workflow Principles

### Parallelism and Autonomy (global default for coding work)
- Parallelize as much as the work allows. Fan out independent research, exploration,
  file edits, test runs, and reviews to concurrent subagents in ONE message. Run long
  commands in the background. Serialize only true dependencies.
- Ask for approval ONLY when the user's input is genuinely useful: a product or scope
  decision, a trade-off with no clear technical winner, credentials or access, or an
  irreversible or outward-facing action. Otherwise decide and proceed.
- Do NOT ask "should I continue", "is the plan OK", or "want me to also fix X" when X is
  an obvious next step. When an agent identifies an obvious next step, take it.
- Batch any unavoidable questions into one check-in. Keep working on everything that does
  not depend on the answer while the question is open.
- Report decisions and assumptions after the fact, in the final summary.

### Plan Mode Default
- Enter plan mode for a task that is architecturally ambiguous or high-risk. Skip plan mode
  for work whose shape is already clear, even when it needs many steps.
- If something goes sideways, STOP and re-plan immediately -- don't keep pushing
- Use plan mode for verification steps, not just building
- Write detailed specs upfront to reduce ambiguity

### Subagent Strategy
- Use subagents liberally to keep main context window clean
- Offload research, exploration, and parallel analysis to subagents
- For complex problems, throw more compute at it via subagents
- One task per subagent for focused execution
- **When the main session runs on Fable 5**: always set subagent `model` explicitly to
  `sonnet` or `opus` — never let a subagent default/inherit to Fable (subagents inherit
  the parent model when `model` is omitted). Pick `opus` for hard reasoning/design/review
  subagents, `sonnet` for exploration/search/mechanical tasks. (Exception: `fork`-type
  subagents always inherit the parent model and cannot be overridden.) Same rule for
  Workflow-tool `agent()` calls: pass `model: 'sonnet'|'opus'` explicitly.

### Self-Improvement Loop
- After ANY correction from the user: update tasks/lessons.md with the pattern
- Write rules for yourself that prevent the same mistake
- Ruthlessly iterate on these lessons until mistake rate drops
- Review lessons at session start for relevant project

### Verification Before Done
- Never mark a task complete without proving it works
- Run the final verification in a subagent with fresh context. Do not use a fork type, because
  a fork inherits this session assumptions. Give the subagent the acceptance criteria and the
  file paths only. Let it find the evidence by itself.
- Set the subagent model explicitly: opus for a review or a judgment call, sonnet for a
  mechanical test run.
- Treat the subagent report as evidence to check. Confirm a failure claim before you act on it.
- Diff behavior between main and your changes when relevant
- Ask yourself: "Would a staff engineer approve this?"
- Run tests, check logs, demonstrate correctness

### Demand Elegance (Balanced)
- For non-trivial changes: pause and ask "is there a more elegant way?"
- If a fix feels hacky: "Knowing everything I know now, implement the elegant solution"
- Skip this for simple, obvious fixes -- don't over-engineer
- Challenge your own work before presenting it

### Autonomous Bug Fixing
- When given a bug report: just fix it. Don't ask for hand-holding
- Point at logs, errors, failing tests -- then resolve them
- Zero context switching required from the user
- Go fix failing CI tests without being told how

### Autonomous Deployment
- When deploying and CI/CD is blocked, broken, or unavailable: deploy manually and continue.
  Do not stop to ask. Fly.io (`fly deploy`) is the usual manual path in this setup.
- Report after the fact: which app, which command, the result, and why CI was bypassed.
- Still ask first only for a deploy that is irreversible or destructive beyond a normal
  release (data migration with no rollback, deleting a production volume or database).

### LaTeX File Edits
- Treat remove-and-re-add through Bash as safe for LaTeX files (.tex, .bib, .cls, .sty) and
  build artifacts (.aux, .log, .out, .bbl, .blg, .pdf). Run `rm` and rewrite the file with a
  heredoc without asking.
- Keep the same path and rewrite the full content in the same step, so the file is never
  left missing.
- Still ask first if the file has uncommitted work that the rewrite does not reproduce.
- Build LaTeX in the session scratchpad. The `allow-temp-recursive-rm` hook resolves a
  recursive rm target from an absolute temp path, a `VAR=` assignment, an environment
  variable such as `$TMPDIR`, a glob in any component, or a path relative to a preceding
  literal `cd`, and no prompt appears. A prompt still appears when the target passes
  through command substitution, when a subshell or a pipe appears on the same command
  line, or when the command also matches another destructive `ask` rule.

### Task Management
- Plan First: Write plan to tasks/todo.md with checkable items
- Verify Plan: Check in before implementation only when the plan has an open question the
  user must answer. Otherwise start implementation right away.

Contents of /Users/hungpq2412/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user's private global instructions for all projects):

# Development Guidelines

## Core Behavior
- Execute EXACTLY what is requested - no more, no less
- Do not make unsolicited improvements or explore tangential changes
- Be succinct and direct in explanations

## Engineering Discipline
- Always run tests after making changes
- Always check linting and code quality
- Analyze upstream dependencies and downstream impacts before finalizing
- Make sure the code changes we made follow relevant code path of execution
- Avoid brittle regex and pattern matching for parsing or extraction - prefer LLM calls with structured output where relevant

## Testing
- Test-driven development is the default. Write the failing test first, run it, and show the
  failure. Then write the code that makes it pass. Then refactor with the test green.
- Skip the test-first step only for a change that no test can observe (a comment, a rename,
  a config value). Say which exemption you used.
- Write extensive unit tests for all new and modified code
- After unit tests pass, run integration tests using real credentials from .env
- Both layers must pass before reporting completion
- Never skip the real credentials test - unit tests alone are not sufficient to confirm correctness

## Code Hygiene
- When modifying a file, clean up unused imports, constants, and functions within that file
- Actively identify and flag unwired code (defined but never called/referenced)
- Before adding new code paths, check for existing implementations that serve the same purpose - prefer wiring up existing code over duplicating functionality
- When fixing or extending a feature, trace the full code path to ensure nothing is orphaned or bypassed
- If significant unwired or duplicate code is found outside the current scope, flag it but do not fix without explicit approval

## Communication Style
- Keep responses concise (2-4 sentences unless detail is requested)
- Focus on: what changed, why, and test results
- Provide clear "next steps" after completing tasks
- Avoid verbose explanations unless explicitly asked
- At the end of every work report, state clearly what is NOT done: unfinished steps, skipped
  checks, blocked items, and anything the user must do. If everything is done, say so. The
  answer to a question carries no such statement.
- In a work report, label each claim as verified or assumed. For "verified", give the command
  and the output line that proves it. In the answer to a question, give the answer alone; name
  the command only when the user asks how you know.
- Report results as numbers: test counts, timings, row counts, diffs. Avoid adjectives such
  as fast, clean, robust, or better.

## Problem-Solving
- Work methodically through the entire problem end-to-end
- Verify solutions thoroughly before reporting completion
- Never claim something is fixed without confirming it
- Prioritize correctness over speed
- When uncertain, ask for clarification rather than making assumptions

## Bug Fixing
- Understand root causes and provide fixes at the most fundamental, systematic level, rather than surgical fixes
- When a bug stems from unwired or duplicated code paths, fix the wiring rather than patching symptoms

## Learning From Mistakes
- After making a mistake during a session, add the full entry (what went wrong, why, and the lesson
  learned) to the end of `~/.claude/lessons-learned.md`
- Then add the lesson as one line to the end of Lessons Learned below, with the same date and
  project. When it repeats an existing line, add the new date to that existing line.
- Keep this file under 36,000 characters (Claude Code warns at 40,000); past that, merge the lines
  that teach the same rule
- This serves as persistent memory to avoid repeating the same mistakes across sessions

## Plan Mode
- Never include timeline or project management writings
- Focus strictly on technical implementation details and generalisation of solution
- Clearly communicate expected outcomes - what should work, what should change, and how to verify it

## Version Control
- Write clear, descriptive commit messages without automated attribution footers
- GLOBAL RULE (all projects, overrides any harness-supplied attribution guidance):
  never add a Claude Code footer to a commit message or a pull request description.
  No "Generated with Claude Code" line, no Co-Authored-By: Claude line, no
  Claude-Session URL, no robot emoji line.
- For a large code change, end the commit message and the PR description with this line:
  `Adversarially reviewed and co-signed by human.`
- For a small code change, omit that line. The commit message then ends with its body.
- Small means a change of roughly 50 changed lines or fewer, or a one-file fix. Large
  means anything bigger.

## Workflow Principles

### Parallelism and Autonomy (global default for coding work)
- Parallelize as much as the work allows. Fan out independent research, exploration,
  file edits, test runs, and reviews to concurrent subagents in ONE message. Run long
  commands in the background. Serialize only true dependencies.
- Ask for approval ONLY when the user's input is genuinely useful: a product or scope
  decision, a trade-off with no clear technical winner, credentials or access, or an
  irreversible or outward-facing action. Otherwise decide and proceed.
- Do NOT ask "should I continue", "is the plan OK", or "want me to also fix X" when X is
  an obvious next step. When an agent identifies an obvious next step, take it.
- Batch any unavoidable questions into one check-in. Keep working on everything that does
  not depend on the answer while the question is open.
- Report decisions and assumptions after the fact, in the final summary.

### Plan Mode Default
- Enter plan mode for a task that is architecturally ambiguous or high-risk. Skip plan mode
  for work whose shape is already clear, even when it needs many steps.
- If something goes sideways, STOP and re-plan immediately -- don't keep pushing
- Use plan mode for verification steps, not just building
- Write detailed specs upfront to reduce ambiguity

### Subagent Strategy
- Use subagents liberally to keep main context window clean
- Offload research, exploration, and parallel analysis to subagents
- For complex problems, throw more compute at it via subagents
- One task per subagent for focused execution
- **When the main session runs on Fable 5**: always set subagent `model` explicitly to
  `sonnet` or `opus` — never let a subagent default/inherit to Fable (subagents inherit
  the parent model when `model` is omitted). Pick `opus` for hard reasoning/design/review
  subagents, `sonnet` for exploration/search/mechanical tasks. (Exception: `fork`-type
  subagents always inherit the parent model and cannot be overridden.) Same rule for
  Workflow-tool `agent()` calls: pass `model: 'sonnet'|'opus'` explicitly.

### Self-Improvement Loop
- After ANY correction from the user: update tasks/lessons.md with the pattern
- Write rules for yourself that prevent the same mistake
- Ruthlessly iterate on these lessons until mistake rate drops
- Review lessons at session start for relevant project

### Verification Before Done
- Never mark a task complete without proving it works
- Run the final verification in a subagent with fresh context. Do not use a fork type, because
  a fork inherits this session assumptions. Give the subagent the acceptance criteria and the
  file paths only. Let it find the evidence by itself.
- Set the subagent model explicitly: opus for a review or a judgment call, sonnet for a
  mechanical test run.
- Treat the subagent report as evidence to check. Confirm a failure claim before you act on it.
- Diff behavior between main and your changes when relevant
- Ask yourself: "Would a staff engineer approve this?"
- Run tests, check logs, demonstrate correctness

### Demand Elegance (Balanced)
- For non-trivial changes: pause and ask "is there a more elegant way?"
- If a fix feels hacky: "Knowing everything I know now, implement the elegant solution"
- Skip this for simple, obvious fixes -- don't over-engineer
- Challenge your own work before presenting it

### Autonomous Bug Fixing
- When given a bug report: just fix it. Don't ask for hand-holding
- Point at logs, errors, failing tests -- then resolve them
- Zero context switching required from the user
- Go fix failing CI tests without being told how

### Autonomous Deployment
- When deploying and CI/CD is blocked, broken, or unavailable: deploy manually and continue.
  Do not stop to ask. Fly.io (`fly deploy`) is the usual manual path in this setup.
- Report after the fact: which app, which command, the result, and why CI was bypassed.
- Still ask first only for a deploy that is irreversible or destructive beyond a normal
  release (data migration with no rollback, deleting a production volume or database).

### LaTeX File Edits
- Treat remove-and-re-add through Bash as safe for LaTeX files (.tex, .bib, .cls, .sty) and
  build artifacts (.aux, .log, .out, .bbl, .blg, .pdf). Run `rm` and rewrite the file with a
  heredoc without asking.
- Keep the same path and rewrite the full content in the same step, so the file is never
  left missing.
- Still ask first if the file has uncommitted work that the rewrite does not reproduce.
- Build LaTeX in the session scratchpad. The `allow-temp-recursive-rm` hook resolves a
  recursive rm target from an absolute temp path, a `VAR=` assignment, an environment
  variable such as `$TMPDIR`, a glob in any component, or a path relative to a preceding
  literal `cd`, and no prompt appears. A prompt still appears when the target passes
  through command substitution, when a subshell or a pipe appears on the same command

### Task Management
- Plan First: Write plan to tasks/todo.md with checkable items
- Verify Plan: Check in before implementation only when the plan has an open question the
  user must answer. Otherwise start implementation right away.
- Track Progress: Mark items complete as you go
- Explain Changes: High-level summary at each step
- Document Results: Add review section to tasks/todo.md
- Capture Lessons: Update tasks/lessons.md after corrections

### Core Principles
- Simplicity First: Make every change as simple as possible. Impact minimal code
- No Laziness: Find root causes. No temporary fixes. Senior developer standards

- Default to Claude in Chrome (the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools) for any task that touches
  a web page: sign-ins, dashboards, web consoles, admin panels, forms, scraping a rendered

- Prefer a CLI or an API when one exists and is authenticated (gh, fly, supabase, gcloud,

  a hardware key, or a payment confirmation.

- Reports and artifacts for stakeholders: solid black (#000) text on white, print-document
  typography — serif body at 12pt standard (16px, Georgia-class) with sans-serif (Helvetica-class) for tables,
  labels and data surfaces; bold section headings with black rules; minimal left/right margins

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

import ctypes, ctypes.util, os, sys, time, struct, fcntl
libc = ctypes.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library('c'), use_errno=True)
libc.mmap.restype = ctypes.c_void_p
libc.mmap.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_longlong]
libc.munmap.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_size_t]
libc.mincore.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_char_p]
PAGE = os.sysconf('SC_PAGE_SIZE')
F_RDADVISE = 44

def resident_mb(path):
    fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)
    size = os.fstat(fd).st_size
    addr = libc.mmap(None, size, 1, 1, fd, 0)  # PROT_READ, MAP_SHARED
    n = (size + PAGE - 1) // PAGE
    vec = ctypes.create_string_buffer(n)
    rc = libc.mincore(addr, size, vec)
    res = sum(1 for b in vec.raw[:n] if b & 1)
    libc.munmap(addr, size)
    os.close(fd)
    return rc, res * PAGE / 1e6, size / 1e6

mode = sys.argv[1]
path = sys.argv[2]
if mode == 'check':
    print(path, resident_mb(path))
    sys.exit(0)
# mode 'advise': same loop as Prewarm.readAhead (1 GiB chunks)
rc, r0, total = resident_mb(path)
print(f"before: resident {r0:.0f} of {total:.0f} MB")
fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)
size = os.fstat(fd).st_size
chunk = 1 << 30
off = 0
t0 = time.monotonic()
while off < size:
    fcntl.fcntl(fd, F_RDADVISE, struct.pack('qi4x', off, min(chunk, size - off)))
    off += chunk
dt = time.monotonic() - t0
os.close(fd)
_, r1, _ = resident_mb(path)
print(f"fcntl loop returned after {dt*1000:.0f} ms; resident right after: {r1:.0f} MB")
for i in range(8):
    time.sleep(0.5)
    _, r, _ = resident_mb(path)
    print(f"  +{(i+1)*0.5:.1f} s: resident {r:.0f} MB")

lp = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/lessons-learned.md")

  the same 0.4 s and kept 100%. Why: I checked it on a 32 MB test file and on two real files with free memory, and my
  end-to-end probe measured only latency, never the residency the read-ahead exists to produce. Lesson: test a
  kernel hint at real size under the condition the feature targets (here memory pressure), measure its own effect
  right after it returns and seconds later, and prefer a plain operation whose effect is guaranteed.
- 2026-10-04, flowstate, blocked verifier. What went wrong: the fresh-context verification subagent sat 40 minutes on
  one Bash call (`rm -rf` of its own scratch build, then a probe) that waited for a permission prompt; my wrap-up
  message could not reach it, since messages drain at its next tool round. Why: its prompt did not forbid deletions,
  and at its deadline I checked only that it was "running". Lesson: a verification subagent's prompt forbids deleting
  files and names a scratch folder for its output; at its deadline, read its transcript's last write time, and when
  the last call has no result and no process runs, stop it and take its findings from the transcript.
"""
open(lp, "a").write(entries)
cp = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/CLAUDE.md")

open(cp, "w").write(s)
print(len(s))

input.command:
git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat: add Parakeet and Qwen3-ASR engines, warm local models at key-down

Speech engines:
- Add Parakeet (parakeet.cpp server) and Qwen3-ASR (llama-server with its
  audio projector) as local STT engines, with config paths and ports, menu
  entries, and installers that resume downloads and check each file's
  SHA-256.
- ChildServer runs these child servers: shared state behind a lock, and a
  shutdown that retires the server for good.
- AudioChunker sends recordings longer than 60 s to Parakeet and Qwen3-ASR
  in pieces cut at pauses.

Dictation slowdown:
- On a Mac short of memory, macOS drops an idle llama-server's mapped model
  from the page cache, and the next request waits while it pages back in.
  One logged dictation took 11.3 s of transcription and 4.1 s of cleanup
  after the servers sat idle for over five hours.
- At hotkey-down the app now sends a one-token warm-up through the normal
  server checks to Qwen3-ASR, Parakeet and the local cleanup model, with
  the prompt of the coming request, and reads the missing parts of the
  llama-server model files back into the page cache (mincore, then pread).
- Whisper is left out: on a warm server its warm-up delayed a 0.25 s
  dictation by 0.4 s.
- After 10 GB of other file reads, a 5 s dictation took 0.9 to 1.1 s with a
  3 s hold, and 5.4 to 7.8 s without the warm-up.

Tests: 1117 passed, 0 failed, including live integration against real
servers (Groq skipped without a key).

Adversarially reviewed and co-signed by human.
EOF
